reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Infantile haemangiomas are the commonest benign tumours of infancy and follow a characteristic course: often absent or subtle at birth, they proliferate over the first months of life, then slowly involute over subsequent years
Superficial lesions are bright red and lobulated (the strawberry appearance), while deeper ones appear as bluish, soft, compressible swellings with little surface change
They are more frequent in premature and low-birth-weight infants and in girls, and most are uncomplicated and need only reassurance and monitoring
The key management question is whether a lesion is high-risk by virtue of its site, size, number, or growth, since early treatment can prevent lasting complications
Beta-blocker therapy has transformed treatment of problematic haemangiomas, with intervention prioritised during the proliferative phase when it is most effective
Periocular lesions can obstruct vision and cause amblyopia, and airway involvement (suggested by a beard-distribution facial lesion with stridor) can be life-threatening
Ulceration is the most frequent complication and is painful, prone to infection, and can scar, so it needs prompt wound care and pain control
Multiple cutaneous haemangiomas raise the possibility of visceral (especially hepatic) involvement and warrant imaging
reference.pathophysiology: Infantile haemangiomas are proliferations of endothelial cells that uniformly express the marker GLUT1, distinguishing them from vascular malformations and other vascular tumours. During the proliferative phase there is rapid, disorganised angiogenesis with plump endothelial cells forming densely cellular masses; hypoxia-driven and angiogenic signalling pathways, including vascular endothelial growth factor mechanisms, are implicated. Over time the lesion enters an involuting phase in which the vascular channels are gradually replaced by fibrofatty tissue. The natural rise and fall in growth explains why timing of intervention matters and why many lesions ultimately regress spontaneously.
additionalDifferentials: Vascular malformations (capillary, venous, or lymphatic), including port-wine stain
Congenital haemangiomas (rapidly involuting or non-involuting types)
Nasal glioma or encephalocele for midline facial lesions
Dermoid cyst or other soft-tissue tumours
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis in most cases based on characteristic appearance and evolution
Ultrasound with Doppler to characterise deep or ambiguous lesions
MRI to define extent of large, segmental, or deep lesions and detect associated anomalies
Abdominal imaging (liver ultrasound) when multiple cutaneous haemangiomas are present
Assessment for PHACE or LUMBAR/PELVIS-type associations with large segmental facial or lumbosacral lesions
Ophthalmology, ENT, or airway evaluation guided by lesion location
redFlags: Periocular lesions threatening the visual axis and risking amblyopia or astigmatism
Beard-distribution facial haemangioma with stridor or respiratory difficulty suggesting airway involvement
Large segmental facial lesions raising concern for PHACE association (cardiac, cerebrovascular, and ocular anomalies)
Lumbosacral or perineal lesions suggesting underlying spinal or urogenital anomalies
Painful ulceration, bleeding, or signs of infection, and multiple lesions suggesting visceral involvement
reference.prognosis: The great majority of infantile haemangiomas are benign and resolve substantially over the first several years of life, often with little residual change; however, high-risk lesions can cause functional impairment, disfigurement, ulceration, or, rarely, life-threatening complications, and timely treatment improves these outcomes.
pitfalls: Assuming a vascular birthmark is always an infantile haemangioma when a malformation or another vascular tumour is present
Adopting a wait-and-see approach for a high-risk lesion and missing the proliferative window for treatment
Overlooking amblyopia risk from a periocular lesion
Failing to image multiple cutaneous lesions for hepatic involvement
Underestimating the significance of a segmental facial or lumbosacral lesion as a marker of associated anomalies
management: Reassure and monitor uncomplicated lesions, as the great majority regress substantially over the first years of life needing only observation
Initiate systemic beta-blocker (propranolol) for high-risk lesions defined by site, size, number or rapid growth, prioritising the proliferative phase when treatment is most effective
Apply topical beta-blocker (timolol) for small, superficial lesions
Undertake pre-treatment cardiovascular assessment and monitor for hypoglycaemia and bradycardia while on propranolol
Protect vision in periocular lesions with prompt treatment and ophthalmology review to prevent amblyopia
Secure the airway and obtain urgent ENT assessment for beard-distribution lesions with stridor suggesting subglottic involvement
Perform liver ultrasound when multiple cutaneous haemangiomas are present, and screen large segmental lesions for PHACE or LUMBAR/PELVIS associations
Refer complex, ulcerated or syndromic lesions to a multidisciplinary vascular anomalies team
